--- jupyter: stats --- # Dimension Reduction with PCA {#sec-unsupervised-pca} Dimension reduction replaces $p$ original predictors, or features, with a smaller number $m0$. The columns of $V$ are the loadings. The score matrix is $$ Z=XV=UD. $$ Therefore: | Quantity | Matrix | Space | Interpretation | |---|---|---|---| | Loadings | $V$ | feature space $\mathbb R^p$ | principal directions, or rotated axes | | Scores | $Z=UD$ | observation space $\mathbb R^n$ | transformed coordinates of observations | | Normalized scores | $U$ | observation space $\mathbb R^n$ | unit-length directions of score vectors | | Singular values | $D$ | -- | scaling, or spread, of each component | | Component variances | $D^2/(n-1)$ | -- | variance explained by each component | Because $$ \frac{1}{n-1}X^\top X = V\frac{D^2}{n-1}V^\top, $$ PCA is also the eigen-decomposition of the sample covariance matrix. This is why [Chapter 1](../1/dr.qmd) defined $v_k$ as an eigenvector of $X^\top X$: the SVD, covariance eigen-decomposition, and variance-maximization definitions are three views of the same object. ## PCA as Matrix Approximation Keeping the first $m$ components gives $$ X_m=U_mD_mV_m^\top=Z_mV_m^\top. $$ This is not merely a convenient approximation. Among all matrices $A$ of rank at most $m$, truncated PCA solves $$ X_m = \argmin_{\rank(A)\le m} \norm{X-A}_F^2. $$ The reconstruction error is $$ \norm{X-X_m}_F^2 = \sum_{j=m+1}^r d_j^2. $$ Thus PCA can be understood in three equivalent ways: - find directions of maximum projected variance; - diagonalize the covariance matrix; - find the best low-rank reconstruction under squared error. ### Visualizing Reconstruction ::: {#9b2f2cc8 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} pca_1d = PCA(n_components=1) score_1d = pca_1d.fit_transform(X_centered) X_reconstructed = pca_1d.inverse_transform(score_1d) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 6)) ax.scatter( X_centered[:, 0], X_centered[:, 1], alpha=0.5, label="observations", ) ax.scatter( X_reconstructed[:, 0], X_reconstructed[:, 1], s=18, color="C1", label="rank-1 reconstruction", ) for x, x_hat in zip(X_centered[::5], X_reconstructed[::5]): ax.plot( [x[0], x_hat[0]], [x[1], x_hat[1]], color="grey", linewidth=0.8, ) ax.set_xlabel("x1") ax.set_ylabel("x2") ax.set_title("Projection and Rank-1 Reconstruction") ax.axis("equal") ax.legend(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](dimensionr_files/figure-html/cell-4-output-1.png){width=513 height=523} ::: ::: The reconstructed points lie on the first principal direction. Their residual distances are the information discarded by the one-dimensional representation. ## Centering and Scaling Centering is essential. Without centering, the leading singular direction can reflect the location of the data cloud relative to the origin rather than variation around the sample mean. `sklearn.decomposition.PCA` centers features automatically, but it does not scale them to unit variance. Whether to scale depends on the meaning of the variables: - scale when units or numerical spreads are not comparable; - retain the original scale when magnitude and variance are meaningful; - state the choice because it changes the principal directions. ::: {#63ed334f .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X_original) pca_centered = PCA(n_components=2).fit(X_original) pca_scaled = PCA(n_components=2).fit(X_scaled) pd.DataFrame( { "centered only": pca_centered.explained_variance_ratio_, "centered and scaled": pca_scaled.explained_variance_ratio_, }, index=["PC1", "PC2"], ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}
centered only centered and scaled
PC1 0.967706 0.964569
PC2 0.032294 0.035431
``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-caution} ## PCA is sensitive to preprocessing Changing units, applying a transformation, or adding many noisy features changes the covariance matrix and therefore changes the PCA representation. ::: ## Explained Variance and Choosing a Dimension The variance explained by component $j$ is $$ \lambda_j=\frac{d_j^2}{n-1}. $$ Its explained variance ratio is $$ \frac{\lambda_j}{\sum_{\ell=1}^r\lambda_\ell}, $$ and the cumulative ratio for the first $m$ components is $$ \frac{\sum_{j=1}^m d_j^2} {\sum_{j=1}^r d_j^2}. $$ For unsupervised PCA, $m$ may be chosen using: - a scree plot or visible elbow; - a target cumulative explained variance; - reconstruction error; - downstream clustering stability; - the dimension needed for a particular visualization. This is the same explained-variance calculation introduced in [Chapter 1](../1/dr.qmd), but the selection criterion changes with the task. In PCR and PLS, $m$ should be chosen by cross-validation against the response because the goal is prediction. In this chapter there is no response, so the choice of $m$ must be justified by the representation goal: compression, reconstruction, visualization, or a downstream unsupervised analysis such as clustering. ## PCA on the Digits Data The handwritten digits dataset has 64 features, one for each pixel in an $8\times8$ image. ::: {#32f77aa7 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} from sklearn.datasets import load_digits digits = load_digits() X_digits = digits.data y_digits = digits.target X_digits.shape ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` (1797, 64) ``` ::: ::: Fit PCA and inspect cumulative explained variance. ::: {#ab365c6d .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} digits_pca = PCA().fit(X_digits) cum_ratio = np.cumsum(digits_pca.explained_variance_ratio_) plt.plot(np.arange(1, len(cum_ratio) + 1), cum_ratio) plt.axhline(0.90, color="C1", linestyle="--", label="90%") plt.xlabel("number of components") plt.ylabel("cumulative explained variance") plt.title("Digits: Cumulative Explained Variance") plt.legend(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](dimensionr_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.png){width=589 height=449} ::: ::: The number of components needed to explain at least 90% of the sample variance is: ::: {#f12a7bcf .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} np.searchsorted(cum_ratio, 0.90) + 1 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` np.int64(21) ``` ::: ::: For visualization, retain two components. ::: {#b4049163 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} digits_2d = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X_digits) fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 6)) scatter = ax.scatter( digits_2d[:, 0], digits_2d[:, 1], c=y_digits, cmap="tab10", s=10, alpha=0.7, ) ax.set_xlabel("PC1 score") ax.set_ylabel("PC2 score") ax.set_title("Digits Projected onto Two Principal Components") ax.legend(*scatter.legend_elements(), title="digit", ncol=2); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](dimensionr_files/figure-html/cell-9-output-1.png){width=670 height=523} ::: ::: The labels are used only to interpret the plot. PCA itself receives only `X_digits`. ## Loadings Loadings describe how the original predictors form each component. This is the same meaning as in PCR: $$ Z_j = v_{1j}X_1+\cdots+v_{pj}X_p. $$ The new point here is interpretive rather than algebraic. In supervised PCR, loadings matter because they tell us which linear combinations become regression predictors. In unsupervised PCA, loadings matter because they tell us what structure the reduced representation is actually preserving. For image data, a loading vector can be reshaped back to the image dimensions. ::: {#4382b928 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} digits_pca_10 = PCA(n_components=10).fit(X_digits) fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 5, figsize=(10, 4)) for j, ax in enumerate(axs.ravel()): ax.imshow( digits_pca_10.components_[j].reshape(8, 8), cmap="coolwarm", ) ax.set_title(f"PC{j + 1}") ax.axis("off") plt.tight_layout(); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](dimensionr_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.png){width=931 height=377} ::: ::: Positive and negative loading regions describe contrasting pixel patterns. The sign of a loading is arbitrary: multiplying both a loading and its scores by $-1$ represents the same component. ## PCA Before Clustering PCA is not a clustering method, but it is often used before clustering: 1. standardize or otherwise preprocess the features; 2. fit PCA; 3. retain a chosen number of components; 4. cluster the score vectors. This can remove low-variance noise and reduce computation. It can also make distance-based clustering more stable when many original variables are highly correlated. However, PCA preserves high-variance directions, not necessarily cluster separation. This is the unsupervised analogue of the PCR limitation emphasized in [Chapter 1](../1/dr.qmd): directions with large variance in $X$ are not always the directions most relevant for the later task. ::: {#855b5522 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} rng = np.random.default_rng(2) n = 300 low_variance_signal = np.repeat([-0.35, 0.35], n // 2) high_variance_noise = rng.normal(scale=4, size=n) X_hidden = np.column_stack( [ high_variance_noise, low_variance_signal + rng.normal(scale=0.08, size=n), ] ) y_hidden = np.repeat([0, 1], n // 2) hidden_scores = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(X_hidden) fig, axs = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 4)) axs[0].scatter(X_hidden[:, 0], X_hidden[:, 1], c=y_hidden, s=18) axs[0].set_xlabel("high-variance noise") axs[0].set_ylabel("low-variance cluster signal") axs[0].set_title("Original Features") axs[1].scatter(hidden_scores[:, 0], hidden_scores[:, 1], c=y_hidden, s=18) axs[1].set_xlabel("PC1") axs[1].set_ylabel("PC2") axs[1].set_title("PCA Scores"); ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![](dimensionr_files/figure-html/cell-11-output-1.png){width=898 height=376} ::: ::: If only PC1 were retained, the cluster information would be discarded. ::: {.callout-caution} ## Variance is not relevance The leading PCs are optimal for reconstructing $X$ under squared error. They are not guaranteed to be optimal for prediction, clustering, or preserving rare subgroups. This is the same limitation that motivates PLS after PCR in [Chapter 1](../1/dr.qmd). The difference is that, in supervised learning, $y$ provides a direct way to define relevance; in unsupervised learning, relevance must be defined by the scientific or analytical goal. ::: ## Summary PCA rotates centered data into orthogonal directions ordered by variance. The loadings $V$ are directions, the scores $Z=XV=UD$ are transformed observations, and $U$ contains normalized scores. These are the same objects used in PCR in [Chapter 1](../1/dr.qmd). The difference is the role they play: PCR treats the scores as predictors for $y$, while this chapter treats the scores as a lower-dimensional representation of $X$ itself. Truncated PCA is the best low-rank squared-error approximation of $X$. In unsupervised learning, the retained dimension should match the representation, visualization, or clustering goal. It need not be the dimension that would be selected for supervised prediction. PCA is linear and its coordinates have interpretable loadings. The next chapter, @sec-embedding, relaxes linearity and focuses on two-dimensional representations designed mainly for visualization.
